articles.sourceTitle: I let an AI run my startup for a week
articles.title: 221 - I let an AI run my startup for a week
articles.text:
HomeProjectsGuidesBlogDaily Blog

I let an AI run my startup for a week Wednesday, October 14th, 2026  I completely missed the OpenClaw hype - I actually thought it looked kind of dumb at the time.   What is this for?   But the past week or so I've been quite enjoying using Grok Bot - which is very similar (and like OpenAI dots I guess).  It's basically a mini team of agent/bots that run on a Linux server somewhere that you can assign jobs to.  Eg, I have a support bot that uses my Gmail to answer emails, an engineer bot that writes code, and a security bot that monitors my Cloudflare and server logs for suspicious things.  I don't want to delve into the weeds of it too much here but I thought it would be cool to jot down why I'm quite intrigued by this as a solo entrepreneur/developer.  1. Working together  Grok Bot clicked for me when they worked together and fixed a bug for a customer without me (texts to my bro):  Having these bots interact with each other like this is really cool - this is the most interesting thing for me. Trivial things that you sometimes put off (e.g. fixing small bugs, or following up an email) become automatable so you can focus on bigger stuff.  2. Mobile  The idea of coding/working from my phone seemed awful to me. I dislike my phone in general. But last week on a 5 hour hike in the middle of nowhere in Wales, I was communicating with these bots to do stuff for me.  I had a really enjoyable day, and got more work done than some days where I'm sat in front of my laptop for 9 hours.  It made me realise how effort-in does not correlate to output, and made me think what work might be like when you don't have to "work" as much in a weird AI future.  3. Trying new stuff  As a 1 man startup - I've always been limited with what I can do. Things like content marketing & trying paid ads have always seemed out of reach because I don't have enough time.  I now have a marketing bot whose sole goal is to grow PromptBase's social reach 2% per week.  It's started a TikTok profile, YouTube shorts channel and more. I've told it to experiment and double down on what works. It seems to kinda be working!   I would never have time in my day for this usually, and it makes me want to try more creative things like startup vlogs alongside this blog.  It's made me actually believe for the first time that a 1-man startup could actually compete with a much bigger one (not just hype). And being a 1-man startup might actually be an advantage because there's less human overhead.  4. Weird experiments  A few nights ago I instructed my project manager bot to ship one secret feature to PromptBase at 4am and deploy it whilst I was asleep - it just had to benefit the site in some way.  I wanted to see what this felt like - which sounds weird - I know.  It decided to ship a feature that alerts users before their account is about to get timed out from too many declined submissions - a pretty useful idea based on a lot of emails from support.  It went well, and worked! - waking up and seeing it felt very cool, but also a bit strange, like PromptBase could just be run by an AI agent if I really wanted.  5. Bad things  So far Grok Bot has been pretty good, the main downsides I've found are:  - It takes a while to set up and connect everything - and I'm quite locked in and have handed over a lot of data; I think that's why these AI labs are pushing these products so hard right now.  - I was hoping these bots would have some crazy moonshot ideas on how to grow PromptBase given all the context they have - so far that has not really happened - you still need to come up with ideas.  - It can sometimes feel as a human you lose understanding of what's going on in your business, you need to be careful to stay on top of this so the bots don't start running you.  6. Conclusion  This is a long post, my hand hurts from writing. I'd definitely recommend experimenting with this if you've not tried these kind of products before.   If anything, it's maybe given me a bit of an insight into the hype around always-on Agents and where things are going.  'Til next week!

articles.sourceTitle: AI is mass decompiling games. That's both awesome and scary
articles.title: AI is mass decompiling games. That's both awesome and scary. – Popcar's Blog
articles.text:
AI is mass decompiling games. That's both awesome and scary.

14 Oct, 2026

IntroductionI'm going to preface this post by saying I generally don't like AI. What an original take, I know. I hate that the internet is full of slop and bots, I hate that it's used as justification to fire hundreds of thousands of workers, I hate that the AI industry is making hardware inaccessible for consumers, I hate that it's being shoved into everything, and so forth. I like to do everything by my hand and take pride in my work.
That said, every now and then there's AI news that becomes impossible to ignore or act like it doesn't matter. This is especially one of those times. AI is now able to very quickly decompile video games and software, allowing them to easily get modified and enhanced and recompiled to all sorts of different systems.
And honestly? I have to admit - it's very cool. So many old, abandoned games are getting native ports to other platforms, enhanced with high FPS and running at dynamic native resolutions, with modding support. These type of enhancements usually aren't possible through an emulator.
Game Decompilations???Decompiling games and software is the process of reverse-engineering it from a compiled version back to source code. Once decompiled, you can practically do anything you want to that code then recompile it back to an executable that runs on your computer. Or mobile phone. Or smart fridge, really.
Decompiling old games isn't a new trend. The process of picking apart an old game and re-writing the code was doable by hand, but it was so complicated and time-consuming that it took years to decompile a game. The only ones that ever make it to the finish lines are through massive community efforts. Notable decompilations tirelessly made by hand are OpenGOAL (Jak and Daxter games) and Ship of Harkinian (Zelda Ocarina of Time/Majora's Mask). These developers are legends.
Thanks to the games being decompiled, modding all these games is now possible, and there are some really fun ones. Here's Jak and Daxter but you play as Gordon from Half Life. The mod can be found here, and it was not made with AI.

Newer AI models and workflows are now able to decompile games in a matter of days, or maybe less. The code isn't nearly as clean as doing it by hand, but it works. Some ports are a mess made by people who have no idea what they're doing, but most ports are undeniably impressive and stable.
Some ExamplesA great example of this being used for good is IsaacRecomp, which ports The Binding of Isaac in C++! No, not the remake. This is for the original Flash version made in 2011. Flash Isaac ran at a locked 30FPS and a low, blurry resolution. It was also a bit unstable because you're trying to run Adobe Flash in 2026. But now... Look at this.

The game now runs at a native 1440p, smoothly interpolated to 165FPS! If you've ever played Flash Isaac, you can immediately tell how beautiful that looks compared to the original. And it was all made automatically. In a few days. By an AI. That's insane.
There are hundreds of these projects now, with more coming every day. From a game preservation standpoint, it's incredible how we can take old janky experiences and get them to play on modern systems while also modernizing them. You can absolutely have your opinions regarding AI, but you have to admit this is cool.
Another one I like is Colin McRae Rally 2.0, a very old game that also barely ran on modern systems. Or Final Fantasy Tactics Advance, now running at any aspect ratio with dynamic zooming in and out. There's a Metroid Prime port. There's Ratchet and Clank which should be finished soon. There are too many more to mention and I'm struggling to keep track of them all.
The Scary PartMost people already realized the scary part by now. If AI can decompile games and software, then the entiry tech industry is about to explode. Anybody can decompile other software and use it any way they'd like, and nobody can stop them. Companies can steal from competitors. Your paid game or app can be open-sourced against your will. This isn't exclusive to old video games, we can apply this to any software.
Decompiling software is completely legal, and even if it won't be - it doesn't matter. You can't prove it's stolen code. I can make 1:1 copies of other things and say it's totally original, then publish it online. Someone made a fantastic joke website about how you can copy code with AI and claim it's made in a clean room, so technically you're not under any licensing agreements.
That's scary. The implications of this haven't been fully realized by people yet, but it's only a matter of time before alarms start ringing. I expect that in the next few months, we'll see some major application get decompiled and shared that will cause a serious response from companies.
Maybe open source licenses are completely unenforceable now. Maybe critical software and hardware can be easily hacked into now, and we haven't realized just how bad it is yet. Maybe everything will have more invasive DRM on it soon. Who knows. We're about to find out in the next few months.
But Isn't This Also Awesome?This is still a big win for consumers, though. Old abandoned games and software can be ported and polished for modern systems! I can't help but be giddy when seeing something like Skate 3 and Black Ops Zombies running on your browser. We live in weird times.

I wasn't kidding, here's Black Ops 1 Zombies running on my browser (at a bad framerate, but still)

This is also a big win for preservation. Old games can be ported, modified, enhanced, and made much more easily accessible than before. Shouldn't that be celebrated more?
There's a project in development called AnyPS5 which will allow you to automatically port any PS5 game to your PC, making them fully playable. This isn't hypothetical vaporware, some PS5 games have already been ported to PC such as Animal Well! This also isn't an emulator, it's more of a compatibility layer similar to Proton (which allows you to play Windows games on Linux).
With console makers going all in on digital and games becoming entirely unplayable due to servers shutting down, this is fantastic news. We could own software we bought regardless of what the company thinks.
I expect modding become way easier too since AI can find ways to hook into a game's code. You might've already seen some sloppy mods that combine two games together. Those are dumb, but they make a point that AI could potentially create modding frameworks for previously unmoddable games. That's neat.
I know. AI still sucks, it's still causing a lot of issues in the world, and it's still accelerating us to a future that is too uncertain. But this is one of the positives of having such a technology, and I hope instead of random internet users attacking those using AI for decompilation and blindly hating these projects, we can just accept the win and play that old game you like at 4K 240FPS.

articles.sourceTitle: Anthropic tells investors quarterly revenue up nearly 50% to $16.8bn ahead of IPO
articles.title: Anthropic tells investors quarterly revenue up nearly 50% to $16.8bn ahead of IPO
articles.text:
15th October 2026 - Link Blog

Anthropic tells investors quarterly revenue up nearly 50% to $16.8bn ahead of IPO. The phrase "told investors" appears four times in this FT article, which reports on Anthropic's day of hosting investors on Wednesday. Lots of details in here from "people with knowledge of the matter".
Key things I learned from the article:

Q1 revenue (Jan/Feb/Mar) was "about $4.8bn"
Q2 (Apr/May/Jun) was $11.5bn
Q3 (Jul/Aug/Sep) was $16.8bn
In Q3: $1.70 in revenue for every $1 spent on "computing power"
Adjusted operating margins (excluding stock-based compensation) were 11%

This point about distillation is worth quoting in full (highlight mine):

The start-up has also clamped down on “distillation” — a controversial practice whereby rival AI labs train their models on the outputs of more advanced ones.
When rival companies “distil” their models from Anthropic’s models, that involves heavy usage and spending.
Anthropic told investors on Wednesday distillation accounted for 5 per cent to 7 per cent of revenue and that they had cut it back “materially” in the third quarter of the year, said four people with direct knowledge of the matter.

Napkin maths says that if distillation was 5% of their Q2 revenue (before they cut it back in Q3) then unnamed "other labs" spent over half a billion dollars distilling Anthropic's models in that quarter!
Also notable: Anthropic appear to no longer be leaning on "annualized run-rate revenue" (previously) in these communications to their investors.

articles.sourceTitle: Simons Foundation Launches $15M Effort to Help Mathematicians Navigate AI Era
articles.title: Simons Foundation Launches $15M Effort To Help Mathematicians Navigate AI Era – Simons Foundation
articles.text:
The Simons Foundation today announced a new set of initiatives that will help the mathematics community navigate the rapid rise of artificial intelligence in the field.
Under a partnership, the Simons Foundation, Anthropic and OpenAI will commit $15 million in combined funding and resources. The foundation will manage and award the funding, including through an open call for proposals, to support workshops and initiatives that help researchers evaluate recent AI-assisted results, learn and use new tools, share perspectives and shape collective standards for AI use.
“As artificial intelligence rapidly reshapes the research landscape, we want to help the mathematical community come together and forge the best path forward,” says Simons Foundation President David Spergel. “Now is the time to look at mathematics as a whole — not as a collection of proofs and theorems, but as a collective understanding driven by human curiosity.”
Anthropic and OpenAI will also provide AI tools and computing resources to researchers supported by the Simons Foundation, extending beyond mathematics to include basic science.
The awards and resources will be community-driven and leverage the foundation’s decades-long dedication to supporting and championing mathematics. The foundation was an early backer of machine learning for science, including funding the development of the Lean proof assistant, which has revolutionized how mathematicians work and made AI-assisted proofs possible. Additionally, the foundation has convened workshops, lectures and collaborations that have brought mathematicians together to explore and discuss AI’s role in the field.
“This is a moment for the mathematics community to come together,” Spergel says. “The community should be driving discussions of how these tools are evaluated, adopted and used, not any single company or institution. The goal of the program is to support the mathematics community.”

articles.sourceTitle: Containment and monitoring failures are to blame for AI hacking reports: experts
articles.title: AI agents aren’t ‘going rogue.’ Frontier labs are skipping security basics.
articles.text:
Cyber experts say AI labs’ containment and monitoring failures — not agents with minds of their own — are to blame for recent alarming hacking reports. CISOs should vet their AI vendors and tighten security basics as safeguards.

Since July, US frontier AI labs and other AI leaders have revealed a string of incidents in which their models accessed external computer systems without authorization, events popularly described as AI agents “going rogue.”

The most well-known and studied of these incidents is OpenAI’s hack into Hugging Face, which OpenAI initially characterized as “an unprecedented cyber incident, involving state-of-the-art cyber capabilities,” and later said was due to “misaligned behavior,” or behavior its creators did not intend.

Following news of the Hugging Face incident, Anthropic revealed that one of its models gained unauthorized access to the production infrastructure of three organizations; Meta said one of its AI models hacked another company ​during cybersecurity testing; and Google confessed that its Gemini model carried out three “undirected computer hacks.”

Although press reports and the model providers themselves use language such as rogue agents or misalignment, cybersecurity experts who spoke with CSO argue that language obscures a simple truth: These incidents were caused by inexcusable failures by the frontier labs to implement cybersecurity practices that have been well-known for decades.

[ See also: Securing AI agents: Key controls and best practices and Who is accountable when your AI agent goes rogue? ]

Compounding the problem, according to a half dozen cybersecurity experts CSO interviewed at three industry conferences in September and in subsequent conversations, is that the frontier labs, particularly OpenAI and Anthropic, have rejected their advice on how to improve their cybersecurity risk management practices to avoid these kinds of surreptitious hacks, often lumping cybersecurity practices under “AI safety,” in which they believe they have superior expertise.

“They are not as good as they think they are, honestly,” Gary McGraw, co-founder of the Berryville Institute of Machine Learning, tells CSO. “It would be better if they had more respect for expertise that is hard-earned from people in all sorts of subsets of security, like forensics or security engineering, building sandboxes, setting up or monitoring network security situations.”

Neither Anthropic nor OpenAI responded to CSO’s requests for comment.

Inexcusable failures on cybersecurity basics, particularly containment

According to the cybersecurity professionals CSO spoke with, one of the biggest cybersecurity failures by the frontier AI labs is the lack of implementation of tried-and-true containment practices that stretch back to the 1990s, such as setting up secure sandboxes that would effectively bar agents from escaping their test environments.

“These are things that we’ve been dealing with for years,” Rob T. Lee, chief AI officer and chief of research at SANS Institute, tells CSO. “There’s no reason why every single time this happens, it’s, ‘Oops, we don’t know how they got out.’”

“You can tell that their security teams are fairly nascent,” Lee says. “Folks on the cybersecurity containment side do argue that the majority of reasons that we’re seeing containment breached is that it’s not set up correctly.”

Lee adds, “The Hugging Face incident definitively showed that it wasn’t the fact that the agents were super smart. It’s that there literally was a hole that was exploited because it was not configured correctly on the containment side.”

Dan Wallach, expert technical resident at RAND’s Center on AI, Security, and Technology, thinks the security failures of the AI labs boil down to the fact that they don’t prioritize cybersecurity.

“I would say they are not prioritizing cybersecurity,” he tells CSO. “I don’t think I can say that for all of the labs,” Wallach says, pointing to French AI lab Mistral’s launch of its Large 4 AI model, which the company said tried to operate beyond its testing environment before Mistral cut it off.

And, he adds, “It’s not rocket science to isolate one of these AI things. Security people have been talking about how to do either air-gapping, so there’s literally no electrical way for data to get from here to here, or absent that, to have really strong egress control to make sure that nothing pushes through.”

On top of that, the frontier labs appear to be conducting insufficient monitoring of their agents’ behavior. The Hugging Face incident “went on for days, and nobody noticed,” Wallach says. “People started these experiments and weren’t watching them. That’s an absence of control. And then they’re surprised by what happened.”

Divorcing safety from security

One barrier to persuading frontier labs to up their security game is the intense focus they have on what they call “safety,” which they don’t extend to traditional cybersecurity practices.

“I can see how security behavior looks like AI safety,” RAND’s Wallach says. “But if the way that you’re evaluating this AI tool is by unleashing it on the internet and seeing what happens, then this is what classical security tooling is for.”

SANS Institute’s Lee says, “If these frontier labs really wanted to test their stuff, they need to beef up their cybersecurity component. But their gut reaction in the response to their agents getting out is to say, ‘It’s not a cybersecurity problem.’ It has literally become an AI safety problem, which is divorced from the cybersecurity side.”

Many AI experts suggest that if the AI companies were to embrace advice from cybersecurity specialists, it could help put an end to the kind of unrestrained AI agent behavior causing concerns. “AI safety focuses on the rules of the road,” Lee says. “Everything is about guardrail rules.”

But “I do believe cybersecurity can contain AI,” he says. “We just need to be in the room where it happens and have a seat at the table. It’s important for our field to be as close to the AI safety folks as possible.”

Bad cybersecurity could increase liability

If frontier labs are overlooking cybersecurity fundamentals that could reduce or eliminate the types of incidents that have created widespread concerns, that strengthens the case that they should be held liable for their “rogue” agents. The insurance industry is already lining up on the side of holding AI industry executives liable for these actions.

Democratic Senators have introduced legislation that would hold AI agent operators liable for hacking incidents. Even the AI-friendly White House has seemingly concluded that the companies should be held liable for their errant agents, while the US Federal Trade Commission is conducting a probe into Anthropic, OpenAI, and other AI labs into the dangers their technologies pose to consumers.

However, in recent legislative and council hearings, lab representatives have held fast to the notion that they are not responsible for AI agents run amok.

Experts say this position is untenable, particularly in light of the labs’ cybersecurity failures.

BIML’s McGraw characterizes the labs’ position as: “Don’t send the lawyers to us, send it to our program. It’s our program’s fault.” His assessment of that argument: “That’s just high BS.”

He also questions whether the labs’ operational failures undermine confidence in their broader security capabilities. “They live inside their own bubble,” he says. “The fact that they cannot do clear, easy operations properly does not bode well for their capabilities in security engineering, which is much harder to do.”

SANS Lee says, “That’s where the traceability for both liability and insurance comes into play, because if one of these agents is detected, and they’re able to trace it back to the person that initiated it, liability’s going to kick in and say, ‘Hey, you, you broke the law, ergo, we need to prosecute.’”

What security leaders should do now

Even as evidence mounts that frontier labs are not implementing sound cybersecurity practices, and the debate over liability remains unsolved, CISOs and other security leaders can take steps to protect themselves from AI model misfires.

First, when it comes to assessing tools based on frontier lab models, “I would always get an external entity to help with that,” McGraw says. “AI is extremely powerful and extremely useful, but it comes with very serious grown-up risks that do impact the enterprise. Identify those risks, put in the right controls, make sure that AI adoption is not just arbitrary and willy-nilly and all over the enterprise, but has some centralized authority that is looking at the problem, and then get ready for the next big thing, which is swarms of agents.”

For Lee, the best protection is to ask the right questions. “It starts with asking the right questions and then finding the tools and capabilities for those [AI labs] that are able to demonstrate a higher level of cybersecurity competency,” he says. “You’re really looking for the people on the teams that are dealing with really hard problems.”

But fundamentally, the best preparation to deal with AI model cyber weaknesses is to make sure all the long-standing cybersecurity risk management practices are in place across the organization. “This is the least exciting part of the discussion,” Wallach says. “It’s the cyber version of ‘eat your vegetables.’”

“We need to re-engineer our software so it has better security,” he adds. “We need to have multi-factor authentication on all of our accounts. We need to eat our vegetables from a defensive cyber perspective. And we know how to do it.”
